newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil GDP juggling improves current account gap.
newsitem.headline: Brazil GDP juggling improves current account gap.

text.p: Brazil will fall well short of most fiscal goals this year, but its current account target is now within range thanks to a new method of calculating gross domestic product.
Analysts say the decision to change methods was primarily motivated by the political concerns of policy-makers, who have seen trade and budget gaps soar beyond expectations this year.
"It's difficult to find any other motive for why they decided to change it at this point," said an economist at a leading Brazilian retail bank who requested anonymity.

The Central Bank announced the change last Friday, saying it brought Brazil's dollar GDP calculations in line with international standards. The bank added that only the current account and other balance of payment figures would be affected by the change.

The new method -- which determines GDP in dollars based on average annual exchange rates rather than purchasing power parity -- significantly boosts the dollar value of Brazil's GDP. Under the new method, the Central Bank said Brazil's GDP through the first seven months of the year would rise to $701 billion from $576 billion.
The new figure should allow the country to close 1996 with a current account gap safely under 3.0 percent of GDP, as has been targeted.
Prior to the change, Brazil was facing a current account gap of close to 3.3 percent, according to some economists.
In announcing the new formula, Central Bank economics department chief Altamir Lopes acknowledged that the timing of the change was "convenient" given the worsening current account picture.
But Lopes said it was purely coincidental, adding that economic stability had allowed Brazil to adopt the new method at this particular time.

The change in methodology drew sharp criticism from the government's statistics institute IBGE, which complained that the Central Bank might now be tempted to tinker with exchange rate policy to manipulate GDP figures.
"The new formula ... is subject to future mismanagement by the monetary authority in currency markets," IBGE coordinator Almir Cronemberg told the financial daily Gazeta Mercantil.
Cronemberg added that the change was "a regression."
But most economists disagreed, accepting the Central Bank's explanation that the new method brought Brazil into line with world standards.
They noted, however, that the government could have avoided accusations it was acting under political motivation by delaying the change until the beginning of next year.

"The point is that the government will now be able to get a better (current account) result without having to improve the public deficit," said Nilson Teixeira, chief economist for Rio de Janeiro investment bank Fonte Cindam.
"But everybody knows they are doing it, so there is no way they are going to fool foreign investors, as some people have suggested," Teixeira said.
